title: Divorce Lawyer Cost: Fees, Retainers and Filing Costs (2026)
description: Divorce lawyer costs explained: hourly vs flat fees, retainers, who pays fees, and verified divorce filing fees for 26 states.
h1: How much does a divorce lawyer cost?
summary: Divorce lawyers usually bill hourly against a retainer; Clio's 2025 data puts the average family-law rate at $344 per hour, so total cost depends mostly on how many hours the dispute takes. Uncontested cases are often handled for a flat fee, while contested custody or property fights can run to tens of thousands. Court filing fees are separate and range from $60 (Virginia's base clerk fee) to $435 (California) among the states we verified. Divorce lawyers cannot charge contingency fees.
body:
What a divorce actually costs you

A divorce bill has three layers: the court's filing fee, your lawyer's fees, and outside costs such as appraisers, mediators, custody evaluators or forensic accountants. The filing fee is fixed and public. The lawyer's fee is the part that varies most, and it depends far more on how much you and your spouse disagree than on the lawyer's hourly rate.

Clio's 2025 data puts the average family-law rate at $344 per hour, against $349 for all lawyers nationally [1]. Those are averages across Clio's users, not quotes; rates in your area can be well above or below them.

Uncontested vs contested: why the gap is so large

In an uncontested divorce, you and your spouse already agree on property, debts, support and parenting. The lawyer's job is to draft or review the agreement and the court paperwork, so many lawyers quote a flat fee. In a contested divorce, every disputed issue can mean discovery requests, depositions, motions, hearings and expert reports, so lawyers bill hourly against a retainer.

Example (illustrative, not a quote): an uncontested case that takes a lawyer 8 hours at the $344 family-law average: 8 × $344 = $2,752. Add California's $435 filing fee [8]: $2,752 + $435 = $3,187.

A contested case with custody and property disputes that takes 60 lawyer hours: 60 × $344 = $20,640, before any appraiser, evaluator or expert fees.

What drives the cost up

  • Disputed custody, especially when a custody evaluation or guardian ad litem is ordered (see child custody lawyer cost).
  • A business, pension or real estate that needs a professional valuation.
  • Hidden or commingled assets that require subpoenas or a forensic accountant.
  • Emergency or temporary-order motions early in the case.
  • A spouse who refuses to exchange documents, forcing motions to compel.
  • Going to trial instead of settling or mediating (see mediation cost guide).

How divorce retainers and replenishment work

Most family lawyers ask for an advance retainer. Under the ABA Model Rules, which most states follow in some form, money paid in advance belongs in a client trust account and the lawyer may withdraw it only as fees are earned or expenses incurred [3]. Each invoice is paid from that balance.

Many fee agreements include a replenishment (or "evergreen") clause: when the balance falls below a set level, you must top it back up, often before the next hearing. Read this clause carefully, because it is how a contested divorce turns into a series of large payments.

Example (illustrative): a $5,000 retainer at $344 per hour covers about 14.5 hours of work ($5,000 ÷ $344 = 14.5). If the agreement requires the balance to stay at $5,000 and the lawyer bills 10 hours in a month (10 × $344 = $3,440), you would owe $3,440 to restore it.

Questions to ask before you sign

  • Is any part of the retainer non-refundable, and what happens to the unused balance when the case ends?
  • What is the hourly rate for the partner, associates and paralegals, and in what time increments do you bill?
  • When does replenishment kick in, and how much notice do I get?
  • Which expenses (process servers, experts, transcripts, mediator) are billed on top?
  • Will you give me a written budget for each phase if the case becomes contested?

Why divorce lawyers cannot work on contingency

ABA Model Rule 1.5(d)(1) bars a fee in a domestic relations matter that depends on securing a divorce or on the amount of alimony, support or a property settlement [2]. That is why you will not find a "no win, no fee" divorce lawyer. Expect hourly billing, a flat fee for defined tasks, or limited-scope help where the lawyer handles only part of the case (see hourly vs flat fee).

Can your spouse be ordered to pay your lawyer?

Some states let the court shift fees from the higher-earning spouse so that both sides can be represented. Two examples:

  • California: Family Code § 2030 requires the court to ensure each party has access to legal representation, including early in the case, and to make findings on whether a fee award is appropriate when one is requested. If those findings show a disparity in access to funds and ability to pay, the court must award fees [4].
  • New York: Domestic Relations Law § 237 creates a rebuttable presumption that counsel fees will be awarded to the less monied spouse, and lets the court award them during the case, not only at the end [5].
Fee-shifting is discretionary and fact-specific. A fee order does not mean your spouse pays everything, and many states use a general "reasonable fees" standard instead. Ask a local lawyer how your state's courts handle it.

Divorce filing fees by state

These are the court fees to file a divorce petition, verified on official court or legislature pages as of October 2026. Several are a statutory base to which counties add surcharges, so call your clerk before filing. States not shown set fees by county or had no verified statewide figure (for example, Indiana fees vary by county).

If you cannot afford the fee, ask the clerk about a fee waiver. Ohio, for example, includes a fee waiver affidavit in its standardized domestic relations forms [6]. See your state page for local legal aid and referral services.

When you may not need a full-service lawyer, and when you do

Limited help can be enough when the marriage was short, there are no children, you have no real estate, business or retirement accounts to divide, and you both agree on everything. Many people use court self-help forms and pay a lawyer only to review the final agreement.

Get a full-service lawyer if there is domestic violence, a dispute over children, a business or significant retirement assets, a spouse who controls the finances or hides information, or a spouse who already has a lawyer. These are the situations where mistakes are expensive and hard to undo.

faq.q: Can I make my spouse pay for my divorce lawyer?
faq.a: Sometimes. California (Family Code § 2030) and New York (DRL § 237) let courts order the spouse with more money to contribute so both sides can be represented, and New York presumes fees go to the less monied spouse. Awards are discretionary, so ask a local lawyer how judges in your county apply the rule.

Advance fees are held in a trust account and drawn down as the lawyer earns them, so the unused part is normally returned at the end. Check the fee agreement for any non-refundable portion and for state rules on it before you sign.

faq.q: Why won't any divorce lawyer take my case on contingency?
faq.a: Professional conduct rules based on ABA Model Rule 1.5(d) prohibit fees that depend on getting a divorce or on the amount of alimony, support or property awarded. Lawyers use hourly, flat or limited-scope fees instead.

faq.q: Is mediation cheaper than hiring two lawyers?
faq.a: Often, because a mediator's time is shared and you avoid motion practice and trial preparation. Many people still pay a lawyer to review the mediated agreement before signing. See our mediation cost guide for how mediators bill.

faq.q: What if I cannot pay the court filing fee?
faq.a: Every court has a process to ask for a fee waiver based on income. Ask the clerk for the form; Ohio, for instance, includes a fee waiver affidavit in its standard divorce forms.
